claims.text: An active-learning machine-learned interatomic potential integrated with thermodynamic integration or enhanced sampling can faithfully reproduce solid- and liquid-phase free energies near melting.
The proposed workflow can retain vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions to the phase free energies.
The proposed workflow will reduce computational cost by roughly one order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD.
The training set will consist of curated ab initio configurations spanning the fusion transition.
A moment tensor potential or neural-network potential will be used as the interatomic model.
Machine-learned interatomic potentials can serve as computationally efficient surrogates for DFT potential energies and forces.
The surrogate potential will accurately capture bonding and vibrational spectra in both ordered solids and disordered fluids.
The surrogate potential will accurately capture high-temperature anharmonicity and electron–vibration interactions.
Strategically selected ab initio snapshots from the transition regime will allow the ML model to interpolate the relevant free-energy landscape rapidly.
Thermodynamic integration or perturbative adjustments can correct residual anharmonic and electron–vibration errors in the ML potential.
Using the surrogate will reduce the number of expensive ab initio evaluations needed for phase-free-energy calculations.
Predicted free-energy differences, melting temperatures, and latent heats will agree with explicit ab initio MD or TOR-TILD results to within approximately 5–10%.
Initial validation will be performed on elemental and binary metallic systems in both solid and melt states near their melting points.
The method requires sufficient high-quality ab initio training data covering both solid and fluid phases.
Extension to multicomponent high-entropy alloys with inadequately represented bonding environments may require additional calibration.
Accuracy is uncertain for systems with extreme anharmonicity, complex electron–vibration coupling, or substantially more complex multicomponent configurations.

The decisive benchmark will compare phase free-energy curves, melting temperature, latent heat, vibrational observables, entropy contributions, and computational cost against explicit ab initio MD or TOR-TILD.
The hypothesis is falsified if errors exceed approximately 5–10% or if computational cost is not reduced by about an order of magnitude.
